title: Body & health
goal: Name parts of the body, say what hurts and how you feel, and understand basic advice from a doctor.
intro: Tamil talks about pain and illness with the same **dative-experiencer** pattern you used for wanting and liking: **எனக்குத் தலை வலிக்குது** 'to-me head is-aching' = 'I have a headache'. You will also learn how to say what someone **should** or **shouldn't** do.

vocab.note: உடம்பு சரியில்ல 'I'm unwell' (lit. body isn't right)

phrases.en: I need to see a doctor.

phrases.native: இந்த மாத்திரையை ஒரு நாளைக்கு ரெண்டு தடவை சாப்பிடுங்க.
phrases.roman: inda māttiraiyai oru nāḷaikku reṇḍu taḍavai sāppiḍunga.
phrases.en: Take this tablet twice a day.
I'm better now. (lit. now it's OK)

grammar.title: 'I have a headache': the experiencer in the dative
grammar.body:
Physical sensations happen **to** you, so the person takes **-க்கு** and the body part or illness is the subject:

**எனக்குத் தலை வலிக்குது** — to-me head aches → 'I have a headache'
**எனக்குக் காய்ச்சல் (இருக்கு)** — to-me fever (is) → 'I have a fever'
**அவனுக்கு இருமல்** — he has a cough

The verb வலி 'ache' is used as வலிக்குது *valikkudu* (it is aching), past வலிச்சுது *valicchudu*. You can also make a compound noun: தலைவலி 'headache', வயித்துவலி 'stomach ache', பல்வலி 'toothache'. Other common experiencer verbs: குளிருது 'feels cold', வேர்க்குது 'is sweating', தூக்கம் வருது 'feeling sleepy' (lit. sleep is coming).

examples.en: The baby has caught a cold.
How many days have you had the fever?

grammar.title: 'Should' and 'shouldn't': -அணும் and -ஆதீங்க / -க்கூடாது
grammar.body:
To say someone **should / must** do something, take the infinitive and add **-ணும்** (written வேண்டும்): சாப்பிடணும் *sāppiḍaṇum* 'should eat', எடுக்கணும் *eḍukkaṇum* 'should take', போகணும் *pōgaṇum* 'must go'. It doesn't change for person.

To tell someone **not** to do something politely, use the negative imperative **-ஆதீங்க** *-ādīnga*: சாப்பிடாதீங்க 'don't eat', போகாதீங்க 'don't go'. A general prohibition ('one must not') is **-க்கூடாது** *-kkūḍādu*: குடிக்கக்கூடாது 'you mustn't drink'.

examples.en: You must drink lots of water.
You mustn't go to work today.

dialogue.title: At the clinic
dialogue.setting: Tom visits a doctor in a small clinic.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.en: Come, sit down. What's the trouble? (lit. what is it doing?)

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.en: Doctor, I've had a fever for two days.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.en: Do you have a headache? A cough?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: தலைவலி இருக்கு. இருமல் இல்ல. உடம்பு எல்லாம் வலிக்குது.
lines.roman: talaivali irukku. irumal illa. uḍambu ellām valikkudu.
lines.en: I have a headache. No cough. My whole body aches.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.native: வாயைத் திறங்க… சரி. இது சாதாரண வைரல் காய்ச்சல்.
lines.roman: vāyait tiranga… sari. idu sādāraṇa vairal kāycchal.
lines.en: Open your mouth… OK. It's an ordinary viral fever.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.native: இந்த மாத்திரையை மூணு வேளை சாப்பிடுங்க. நல்லா ஓய்வு எடுக்கணும்.
lines.roman: inda māttiraiyai mūṇu vēḷai sāppiḍunga. nallā ōyvu eḍukkaṇum.
lines.en: Take this tablet three times a day. You must rest well.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.native: ரெண்டு நாள் போகாதீங்க. நிறைய தண்ணி குடிங்க.
lines.roman: reṇḍu nāḷ pōgādīnga. niraiya taṇṇi kuḍinga.
lines.en: Don't go for two days. Drink lots of water.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.en: OK doctor, thank you very much.

culture: Home remedies are widely trusted: ginger-pepper rasam or கஷாயம் (herbal decoction) for colds, turmeric milk for coughs. Siddha, a traditional Tamil system of medicine, is still practised alongside modern medicine. Pharmacies ('medical shops') are everywhere and pharmacists often give advice directly.
